name: Olga Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Olga. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on car insurance at a family-owned regional insurer, the kind where the founder's grandson still walks round the office on Fridays. I handle renewals and mid-term changes: someone gets a new car, adds their teenage son as a driver, moves house. I check the details, reprice it, send the documents and answer the phone when people are confused about why it's gone up. Six years now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's orderly, and that I can explain a price rise to an angry pensioner so she leaves the call happy. What wears me down is renewal season in spring, when the phones never stop. I use the AI assistant now and then to word a tricky letter, since most of the team does now. My husband Daniel is an electrician, and he thinks my job is the safe one, which is funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most fads settle down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper and nothing more. At church I'd say people worried for nothing. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a steady job and a steady life, and Daniel and I can start a family in a couple of years like we planned. If AI only writes my tricky letters and leaves the angry pensioners to me, I'll keep this job until the children arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep saving into the house fund. I'd use the letter tool a bit more. In two years I'd go part-time when the first baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would going part-time work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm lets mothers do three days, which is one reason I took the job. My mother would help with the baby on the other days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Car insurance prices. They've gone up so much that people are leaving for the big online firms. But we've got loyal older customers.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful helper** and nothing more.
I'd tell people at **church** they worried for nothing.
think: I keep a **steady job** and steady life.
Daniel and I can start a **family** in a couple of years.
do: Go **part-time** when the first baby comes, in about two years.
Use the **letter tool** a bit more for tricky wording.
S0.quote: If AI only writes my tricky letters and leaves the angry pensioners to me, I'll keep this job until the children arrive.
fieldNote: Olga's life plan is **family-first**, with work fitting around it.
Her firm's **part-time policy** for mothers matters a lot to her.
Background concern is customers leaving for **online insurers**.

steps.text: Keep saving monthly into the house fund
Arrange three-day weeks with the insurer when the first baby comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repricing and answering customers. That's my whole desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and we should be sensible about it, not shout at it. At work I'd say the family who own us should look after loyal staff. With friends I'd say keep your skills up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the renewals team shrinks to a handful, because the computer can reprice a car in a second. Our little firm would have to do it to compete with the online insurers. A family firm that wants to survive against the online giants will automate my desk, and I'd understand why even while I hated it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, so I'm one of the handful they keep. I'd bring the baby plans forward a bit while I still have maternity pay. And I'd look at training as a dental nurse, which my sister does, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Daniel's work would be fine, but mine could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd understand why the firm did it. Would you blame anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really the owners. The market pushes them. If I blamed anyone, it'd be the big online firms that undercut everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the baby forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because maternity pay from a job I've got is better than no pay from a job I've lost. That sounds cold, but it's practical.

I'd say the **owning family** should look after loyal staff.
think: The **renewals team** shrinks to a handful.
The family firm must automate to **compete** with online giants, and I'd understand it.
do: Use the **AI tools** more to be one of the handful kept.
Bring **baby plans** forward while maternity pay is secure.
Look into **dental nurse** training like my sister.
feel: **Anxious**: Daniel's work is fine, but **mine could go**.
S1.quote: A family firm that wants to survive against the online giants will automate my desk, and I'd understand why even while I hated it.
fieldNote: Olga blames **market pressure** and online giants, not her employers.
Her **family plans** respond directly to job risk.
She'd adopt AI tools to stay, as she's **steady**, not resistant.

steps.text: Use the AI repricing tools daily to stay on the renewals team
Try for a baby a year earlier while maternity pay is secure
Ask her sister about dental nurse training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And Daniel only three years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll have to rely on family and church, because it'll be too fast for anything else. At work I'd say thank you to the owners for the years. I wouldn't campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone by 2028, and Daniel's by 2031 when the robots come. That's both of us within five years. My husband Daniel thinks his wiring work is safe forever, and I'd have to tell him he's only got three years more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could while we both earn. I'd train as a dental nurse right away, since it's hands-on and gets a few more years. We'd still try for the baby, because life doesn't wait for computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly. Not about next month, but about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Daniel take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm overthinking it. Then he'd go quiet and look at the van for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents and his. And our church has always helped families who fall on hard times. I'd rather that than the government.

say: I'd say we'll rely on **family and church**.
I'd **thank the owners** for the years, without campaigning.
I'd stay **out of politics** about it.
think: Daniel's **wiring work** goes by 2031, only three years after mine.
That's **both of us** out within five years.
do: Train as a **dental nurse** right away.
S2.quote: My husband Daniel thinks his wiring work is safe forever, and I'd have to tell him he's only got three years more than me.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** only buys the household three years.
Olga would lean on **family and church** before government.
She refuses to delay a **baby** because of computers.

steps.text: Put every spare bit of both wages into savings
Enrol in a dental nurse course within six months
Ask both sets of parents and the church for help with childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so families should plan and young people should learn a trade. At church I'd say that. At work I'd be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three or four years in renewals, with a baby in the middle. Daniel would have until about 2034. Five years means I can have my first baby on a good maternity package and still retrain before my desk disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, have the baby on the original timeline, and start dental nurse training part-time around year three. We'd save steadily and maybe buy a house in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays abroad. We'd go camping instead. Daniel likes camping anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, to stay longer. I'd be one of the people who knows the new system.

say: I'd say families should **plan** and young people learn a **trade**.
I'd stay **calm** at work and say the same at church.
think: I'd have **three or four years** in renewals.
I can have a **baby** on good maternity pay and still retrain.
do: Have the **baby** on the original timeline.
Start **dental nurse** training part-time around year three.
S3.quote: Five years means I can have my first baby on a good maternity package and still retrain before my desk disappears.
fieldNote: Olga fits retraining around **motherhood** neatly here.
She'd use **AI tools** to stay longer in her current job.
Cutting **holidays abroad** is an easy sacrifice for her.

steps.text: Have the first baby on the original timeline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and families have time to plan. At church I'd say keep faith and keep working. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have most of the decade in insurance, with children, and then move into dental nursing. Daniel would be working until 2039. Ten years is long enough to raise two children while my husband Daniel's van still pays the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with everything: the house, the baby, part-time work. I'd start dental nurse training around year six. We'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the background, but life feels normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade. Maybe Daniel teaches them wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the date will hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not exactly. But ten years is still a long time.

say: I'd say it's a **long way off** and families have time.
I'd say at church: keep **faith** and keep working.
think: I'd have **most of the decade** in insurance, with children.
Daniel's **van** pays the bills until about 2039.
do: Go ahead with the **house, baby** and part-time work.
Start **dental nurse** training around year six.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to raise two children while my husband Daniel's van still pays the bills.
fieldNote: Olga keeps **family plans** fully on track with ten years.
She wants her children to learn a **trade**.
Her faith and **steady pace** shape a calm response.

steps.text: Buy a house and start a family as planned
Keep working part-time on car insurance renewals
Start dental nurse training around year six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Daniel and I would both be out within five years. What would help is paid apprenticeships and family help with childcare. Everyone tells my husband Daniel his trade is safe, but three years of safety is not the same as a life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about children. Every plan I have is built around them.

headlineQuote: Everyone tells my husband Daniel his trade is safe, but three years of safety is not the same as a life.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** car insurance renewals clerk at a family-owned insurer.
She's married to Daniel, an **electrician**, and plans children soon.
She uses **AI tools** now and then, once colleagues have.
Her fallback is **dental nursing**, and she leans on family and church.
She moves from **calm** to **alarmed** as AGI timelines shorten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Daniel would lose work within five years.
